AI Images

So far in this class we've looked at AI that works with words. This week is about AI that makes pictures: how it works, what people use it for, and how to get better results from it.

Every picture in these slides that isn't a diagram was made by AI for this lesson. Each one comes with the request that made it, so you can see exactly what was asked.

Use the arrow keys or the buttons at the bottom to move between slides.

→

A picture is a grid of numbers

A digital picture is made of tiny colored squares called pixels. They are so small that you don't notice them unless you zoom in.

Each pixel is stored as three numbers: how much red, how much green, and how much blue light to show. Each number goes from 0 (none) to 255 (full). Your screen mixes the three lights to make the color.

Red 255, green 255, blue 255 is white. All three at 0 is black. Everything else is somewhere in between.

So to a computer, a photo is just a very long list of numbers. A picture from an AI image tool is usually 1024 by 1024 pixels. That's about a million pixels, and over 3 million numbers.

Try it: tap anywhere on the parrot to zoom in. Tap a square to see its three numbers, then move the sliders to change that pixel.

The whole picture. The box shows where you zoomed.

Zoomed in: 12 × 12 pixels.

Making a picture is much harder than reading one

Last week's number reader took a small picture and gave back one answer, like "7". That's a lot of numbers in and one answer out.

An image generator goes the other way. You give it a few words, and it has to give back millions of numbers. And they all have to fit together: the fur has to look like fur, the shadow has to fall on the right side, the dog needs four legs.

Picking numbers at random doesn't work. Almost every possible set of numbers just looks like static. The pictures that actually look like something are incredibly rare among all the possibilities.

Try it: press the button to fill the square with random numbers. Press it as many times as you like. You will never see a dog.

Adding noise

Most image generators are built on a simple trick. To understand it, you first need to know what noise is.

Noise means random changes. Take a photo, and to every pixel's numbers, add or subtract a small random amount. The photo gets grainy, like an old TV with bad reception.

Do it again and again, and the photo slowly disappears. In the end there's nothing left but static, the same kind you saw on the last slide.

Going forward like this is easy. Anyone can wreck a photo. The clever part, on the next slide, is teaching a computer to go backward.

Try it: drag the slider to add noise. Watch the pixel numbers change.

Training: learning to remove noise

To train an image generator, you collect a huge number of photos. Each one comes with a short description, called a caption.

Then you play a guessing game, millions of times:

  1. Add noise to a photo. Sometimes a little, sometimes a lot.
  2. Guess. The model sees the noisy photo and the caption, and guesses what the clean photo looked like.
  3. Check and nudge. Compare the guess to the real photo, and nudge the weights so the next guess is a bit closer. This is the same loop as last week.

Notice what happens with a lot of noise. Many different photos could be hidden under that much static, so the best the model can do is a blurry guess. That turns out to be fine, as you'll see next.

Try it: pick how much noise to add and compare the guess to the real photo.

Caption that came with the photo: "A scarlet macaw parrot"

The guesses here are a simulation, made to look like what a trained model produces.

Making a new picture from static

Once the model is good at removing noise, you can use it to make pictures that never existed.

Start with pure static, made up at random. Ask the model what picture might be hiding under it. The first guess is a blurry blob. Remove a little noise in the direction of that guess.

Now the image is slightly less noisy, so the next guess is a bit sharper. Repeat. After 20 to 50 rounds, all the static is gone and a picture is left.

Because the starting static is random, you get a different picture every time, even with the same request. This is like the temperature setting from week 1.

Try it: press "Next step" to remove noise one round at a time. Then press "New static" and run it again.

Request: "A dog on a beach"

This is a simulation. To show the idea, it uses pictures the AI already made. A real model has no finished picture to work toward. At each step, it has to guess one.

How your words steer the picture

During training, every photo came with its caption. So the model didn't just learn "what's under this static?" It learned "what's under this static, if the caption says lighthouse?"

When you make a new picture, your request takes the place of the caption. At every step, your words pull the guess toward a dog, a lighthouse, or a bowl of fruit.

Start from the exact same static with different words, and you end up somewhere completely different.

Image generators that work this way are called diffusion models. DALL-E, Midjourney and Stable Diffusion were all built like this, and many tools still are.

Try it: all three start from the same static. Press "Run" to remove the noise with each request.

The newer way: the chatbot draws the picture itself

In week 1 you saw that a picture can be cut into small square tiles, and each tile treated like a word.

The newest image tools in ChatGPT, Gemini and Meta AI use that idea. There is no separate drawing program anymore. The picture is made by the same kind of model that writes your answers.

OpenAI has said its image model works tile by tile, the way a chatbot writes a sentence word by word. Each new tile is based on your request, the whole conversation, and every tile made so far.

ChatGPT switched to this in 2025. Before that, it passed your request to DALL-E, a separate diffusion model, and you couldn't really talk with it about the picture.

Try it: press "Play" to watch the two methods side by side.

Simplified. Real tiles are much smaller, and the companies don't publish every detail. Many of these systems seem to combine both methods: tiles to plan the picture, and a noise-removal step to paint the fine detail.

Why that matters: it understands what you asked

Older image generators read your request with a fairly small text reader. They picked up the main things, like "cake" and "girl" and "yellow", but often lost track of details. Words in the picture usually came out as gibberish.

When a full language model draws the picture, it brings everything it knows about language and the world. It can follow long instructions, spell words correctly, and use facts, like the order of the planets.

The newest models also plan before they draw. GPT Image 2, released in April 2026, works through the request first, like the thinking models that work through a problem before answering.

Try it: check each picture against the list yourself, then press "Show marks". The small model is a 2026 model too. It's much smaller and faster, and makes the kind of mistakes older tools made all the time.

Why AI pictures still go wrong

An image model makes what looks likely, based on the pictures it learned from. It doesn't check whether the picture is correct. This is the same problem as hallucination in week 1.

So when you ask for something that rarely appears in photos, the model drifts back to what it has seen most.

The newest models get these examples right much more often. But they still make smaller mistakes that are easy to miss: a measurement that's a bit off, a sign with one wrong letter, a hand with an extra finger, a shadow that falls the wrong way. Always look closely before you use a picture.

Try it: for each request, look for the mistake first. Then press "What went wrong?"

Where all those pictures came from

An image model needs an enormous number of pictures with captions. Most came from the public internet. The caption is often the text that a web page put next to or under the picture.

One well-known collection, called LAION-5B, has about 5.85 billion pictures paired with text. It was used to train Stable Diffusion. Newer companies mostly don't say exactly what they used.

If you looked at one picture every second, day and night, getting through 5.85 billion would take about 185 years.

Many of these pictures were made by artists and photographers who were never asked and never paid. Artists and photo companies such as Getty Images have taken AI companies to court over this, and courts in different countries are still working out what the law allows. Some tools, like Adobe Firefly, say they trained only on pictures they had permission to use.

Try it: press the button. Each dot is 10 million pictures.

What people use it for

Here are six everyday uses. Each picture was made with one short request, and some started from an ordinary phone photo.

Try it: tap a picture to see the request that made it.

Changing a photo you already have

You don't have to start from nothing. You can upload a photo and describe what to change: remove something, put it in a new place, change the lighting, make it wider.

Be clear about what should stay the same. "Keep everything else exactly the same" helps a lot.

Even then, compare the two versions carefully. Some tools redraw the whole picture, not just the part you asked about, so small details can shift without you noticing. These examples came out clean, but don't assume yours will.

Try it: drag the slider across the picture to compare before and after.

BeforeAfter

Where to make AI pictures

You don't need a special app. The chat tools you already use for writing can make and edit pictures too. Just ask in the chat, or attach a photo and say what to change.

All of these change often. New versions come out every few months, and free limits go up and down. The details on the right are from October 2026.

For this class, ChatGPT or Gemini is a good place to start.

A short request gets the average picture

For this slide, the same request was typed four separate times: "A dog on a beach."

Look at what came back. A dog could be any breed, any size, doing anything, on any beach, at any time of day. But every single time: a golden retriever, facing the camera, tongue out, at sunset.

This is the lesson from the end of week 1 again. AI leans toward the most common, most expected version of whatever you ask for. If you leave something out, it fills the gap with the average.

So if you have something specific in mind, you have to say it.

Try it: press "Ask again" to see each of the four answers.

Add the details you care about

A good request answers the questions the model would otherwise answer with the average. You don't need special words. Just describe what you see in your head.

  • What: the main thing, and what it's doing
  • Where: the setting
  • Style: photo, watercolor, cartoon, pencil drawing
  • Light: time of day, mood, where the light comes from
  • View: close up or far away, from above or below

You don't need all five every time. Add the ones that matter to you.

Try it: add one detail at a time and watch the picture change. Tap any step to go back to it.

A rough sketch beats a long description

Words are bad at describing where things go. "A tree on the left, a little bigger, and the house further back" gets tiring fast, and the model still has to guess the rest.

A sketch shows it all at once: where each thing is, how big it is, and how it's arranged. The new models really understand pictures you give them, so they can follow your sketch closely.

Your sketch doesn't have to be good. Circles, boxes and stick figures are fine. Draw on paper and take a photo with your phone, or draw on a phone or computer. Attach it and say what it is.

Try it: compare the result from words with the result from a sketch. Then drag the slider to lay the sketch on top of the finished picture.

Other pictures you can give it

A sketch is one kind of picture you can attach. Two others are just as useful:

A photo of your own thing. Your dog, your product, your living room. Words can't describe your exact dog, but a photo can. The model keeps it recognizable and puts it somewhere new.

A picture of a style you like. If you can't name a style, show it. Say "in the same style as this picture" and attach an example.

You can attach more than one at a time, for example a photo of your dog and a painting whose style you like.

Try it: switch between the two examples.

Fix it one step at a time

The first picture is rarely exactly right. Don't start over. Keep chatting and ask for changes, the same way you'd give notes to a person.

  • Change one thing per message. Ask for five changes at once and some of them will get missed.
  • Say what to keep if the model starts changing things you liked.
  • Point to things plainly: "the door", "the dog on the left", "the sky".
  • If it goes off track after many changes, start a new chat. Attach the best version so far and keep going from there.

Try it: press "Next message" and watch what changes and what stays the same.

Is this picture real?

You've seen how realistic these pictures are now. The old giveaways, like extra fingers and garbled writing, are mostly gone. Assume any surprising picture online could be made by AI.

Check where it came from. Who posted it first? Is a trusted news source showing it too? Google Lens and other reverse image searches find where else a picture has appeared.

Look for a hidden label. Many tools now hide a label inside the picture. ChatGPT pictures carry "Content Credentials", a record saying which tool made them. Google adds an invisible watermark called SynthID, and you can upload a picture to Gemini and ask whether Google AI made it. Labels can be lost when a picture is screenshotted or edited, so no label doesn't prove a picture is real.

Be honest with yours. If a picture could be mistaken for a real photo, say it was made with AI. Never make fake pictures of real people.

Try it: choose a picture file from your device. This page looks for Content Credentials inside it. Nothing is uploaded.
